text: hey everybody an interesting Insight from the cognitive science of religion is that what we label religious beliefs tend not to be very deeply held beliefs
they don't tend to influence our intuitive or our subconscious perception of and thinking about ourselves and the
world around us they tend to sit closer to the surface cognitive scientists would call them credences or things that we accept because accepting them is
important to us and a good illustration of this is a series of experiments conducted by Justin Barrett and his colleagues about 20 years ago regarding
theological correctness and how people think about God and uh in this series of experiments they started with participants who were given a
questionnaire about their theological beliefs about God and after filling that out they read some stories about a supercomputer and Superman and God and
things like that and then uh some time was allowed to pass and then they were asked questions about how they recalled the details of
those stories and the majority of participants recalled those details in ways that showed they thought about God
as more like a human being as an anthropomorphic corporeal entity that was limited in time and space and did
not have all knowledge and then they repeated the experiment but before asking the questions about how people
recalled the the stories they reminded them of the results of the questionnaire that they filled out they reminded them
what they said they believed about God and this time when the people were actively thinking about what they said they believed about God the
anthropomorphizing of God dropped way off in other words when people were not actively thinking about theologically
correct beliefs they reverted to what is intuitively natural which is to think about God as anthropomorphic corporeal
Limited in time and space and so on it wasn't until they were actively thinking about what was theologically correct
that those religious beliefs influenced how they thought about God
